📚 Today you learned

IPO Lock-Up Expiration

When a company IPOs, early investors, founders, and employees are usually barred from selling for a set window — typically 90-180 days. When it expires, a huge supply of shares becomes sellable at once, and price often drops even with zero business news. SWMR's -28.4% today is a clean example: a lock-up freed ~59% of shares outstanding for sale, on top of dilution fears from a fresh acquisition. Nothing about the business changed overnight — the float just tripled. This matters for you mainly as a filter: if you ever see a small-cap "cheap" relative to its IPO price, check the lock-up calendar before assuming it's a discount — you might be looking at forced selling, not opportunity. Recent-IPO names deserve an extra step most of your current holdings don't need.

Also today: Float rotation — after a lock-up, watch whether volume normalizes in days (temporary overhang) or stays elevated for weeks (real distribution, avoid catching the falling knife).
